passage:
On the steps of the colony park in Pune, Vijay was complaining again. Megha had gone to a cousin's party without telling him who'd be there. He'd messaged her twelve times.
Sarita, who had known him since they were six, listened to all of it. Then she asked, "Vijay, what are you actually afraid of losing?"
"What? Her, obviously."
"But why would you lose her? Because she went to a party?"
He opened his mouth to argue and nothing came out. He picked at a thread on his jeans for a long time.
"Because..." he said finally, "there are guys who are smarter. Better at everything. I'm scared one day she'll notice I'm not that good."
Sarita nodded slowly. "So checking her phone won't fix that. That's about how you see yourself, not about her."
He didn't answer. But he didn't send a thirteenth message either.

qa.q: How many times had Vijay messaged Megha?
qa.a: Vijay had messaged her twelve times.

qa.q: What fear does Vijay feel underneath the jealousy?
qa.a: Vijay admits being scared he isn't good enough and that Megha will one day notice.

qa.q: Why was Sarita's question a turning point?
qa.a: Asking what he was afraid of losing moved Vijay from blaming Megha to seeing his own self-worth problem, which controlling her cannot fix.

qa.q: How might Megha experience twelve messages during a party?
qa.a: Megha might feel pressured and watched, unable to enjoy her cousin's party without worrying about Vijay's reaction.

grounding: Shows a wiser friend asking a jealous teen what he fears losing, and his admission that the real problem is feeling not good enough.

passage:
"Rupsa said she's studying with Soumik again," Anirban said, kicking the terrace wall.
"Okay," Jeevan said. "And?"
"And I asked her to send a photo of where she was. She didn't."
"Why do you need a photo?"
"To know."
"Know what?"
"That she's... not choosing him."
Jeevan passed him a cup of chai from his mother's tray. "Can I ask you something weird? What are you scared of losing?"
Anirban laughed, then stopped. He looked at the chai for a long time.
"That she'll figure out I'm boring. Soumik's in the quiz team. I'm just... me."
"So the photo isn't really about Rupsa," Jeevan said gently. "It's about you feeling not enough."
"...Yeah."
"Then checking on her won't fix it, na? Maybe tell her you felt insecure, instead of asking for proof."

qa.q: What did Anirban ask Rupsa to send?
qa.a: Anirban asked her to send a photo of where she was.

qa.q: What is Anirban really afraid of?
qa.a: Anirban is afraid Rupsa will find him boring and not enough compared with Soumik.

qa.q: What does Jeevan suggest instead of asking for proof?
qa.a: Jeevan suggests Anirban tell Rupsa honestly that he felt insecure, since checking on her can't fix how he sees himself.

qa.q: What might Rupsa feel when asked for a photo?
qa.a: Rupsa may feel distrusted and controlled, as if she has to prove she isn't doing anything wrong.

grounding: Illustrates a friend's question uncovering that a teen's jealousy comes from feeling not good enough, which controlling his girlfriend cannot fix.

passage:
I didn't expect Wilson, of all people, to be the one who got it.

We were on the terrace after tuition, and I was going on about Lavanya again. How she'd laughed with the new boy in her dance class. How she took forty minutes to reply. How I'd asked to see her messages and she'd gone quiet.

Wilson let me talk. Then he said, "Santosh, what are you actually afraid of losing?"

I opened my mouth to say "her". What came out was, "I'm not good enough for her. She's going to figure it out."

It was so quiet I could hear the pigeons.

Wilson said, "So checking her phone is you trying to fix that?"

I realised it was. And it couldn't. Nothing I found in her phone would make me feel good enough. That problem was mine, not hers.

That night, for the first time, I didn't text Lavanya asking who she was with.

qa.q: Where were Santosh and Wilson talking?
qa.a: On the terrace after tuition.

qa.q: What did Santosh feel when he admitted he wasn't good enough?
qa.a: He felt exposed and afraid, and also a sudden clarity that his checking came from low self-worth.

qa.q: What made Wilson's question a turning point?
qa.a: Asking what Santosh was afraid of losing helped Santosh see the real issue was his self-worth, which controlling Lavanya could never fix.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel when the checking messages stop that night?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and relieved, perhaps a little unsure at first whether it will last.

grounding: When a wise friend asks what he is afraid of losing, Santosh admits feeling not good enough and sees that controlling Lavanya cannot fix his self-worth.

passage:
Coach's note, after Thursday practice

Harish has been distracted for three weeks, checking his phone between drills and missing easy catches. Today he snapped at Ritesh for no reason.

After practice I saw them sitting on the pavilion steps. Ritesh asked Harish what was going on. Harish said his girlfriend, Meenal, kept hanging out with a boy from the debate team, and he'd started asking to see her messages.

Ritesh asked him quietly, "What are you scared of losing, bhai?"

Harish was silent a long time. Then he said, "That I'm not enough. That she'll find someone better." His voice cracked.

Ritesh didn't laugh. He said, "Checking her phone won't make you feel enough."

I spoke to Harish afterwards. I told him I'd noticed he'd been struggling and suggested he meet the school counsellor about the not-good-enough feeling. He agreed to go on Monday. I'll check in with him then.

— Coach Vijay

qa.q: Who did Harish snap at during practice?
qa.a: Ritesh.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when his voice cracked?
qa.a: He felt insecure and afraid, admitting he felt not good enough and feared Meenal would find someone better.

qa.q: What did Ritesh and the coach do that helped?
qa.a: Ritesh asked what Harish was scared of losing and pointed out that checking her phone couldn't fix it; Coach Vijay then suggested the school counsellor for the self-worth worry.

qa.q: How might Meenal have experienced Harish asking to see her messages?
qa.a: She likely felt watched and uncomfortable, even though she had only been with a debate team friend.

grounding: A coach's note shows a wise friend asking Harish what he fears losing, Harish admitting he feels not good enough, and the coach pointing him to the counsellor.

passage:
Friday night

Tanuja asked me something today that I can't stop thinking about.

I was complaining about Pallavi again. How she went to the café with her cousins and a boy from her building, and didn't tell me till after. How I'd asked her twice who else was there, and she got annoyed.

Tanuja put down her samosa and said, "Anand, what are you so scared of losing?"

I said, "Pallavi, obviously."

She said, "No. Deeper."

And I sat there on the canteen bench and it came out: "That I'm boring. That she'll wake up one day and realise she could do better."

Tanuja nodded like she'd known all along. "So asking who she was with won't fix that. You'd just be the boyfriend who checks."

She's right. The problem isn't Pallavi. It's me not feeling like enough. I need to work on that, not on her.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi go without telling Anand until after?
qa.a: To the café with her cousins and a boy from her building.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when the deeper answer came out?
qa.a: He felt exposed and a little ashamed, admitting he fears he is boring and not enough for Pallavi.

qa.q: Why was Tanuja's question more useful than advice about Pallavi?
qa.a: It helped Anand see the real issue is his own self-worth, which checking on Pallavi could never fix.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt being asked twice who was there?
qa.a: She likely felt annoyed and mistrusted, as if an ordinary outing needed explaining.

grounding: Anand's diary shows a wise friend asking what he fears losing, and his realisation that the real issue is his self-worth, which controlling Pallavi cannot fix.
